newsitem.title: USA: U.S. publicly demands firing of Bosnian official.
newsitem.headline: U.S. publicly demands firing of Bosnian official.

text.p: The United States on Friday publicly called for the dismissal of Bosnian Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic as a condition for delivering $100 million worth of military hardware to Sarajevo.
U.S. officials said privately last week the equipment would not be handed over until Cengic was fired because of his alleged ties with Iran.

But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington was now going public because Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation had so far failed to meet promises to sack him. Under the Dayton peace accord, Bosnia was divided into the Federation and a Serb entity.
"The United States has determined that Bosnian Federation Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic personally maintains close ties to Iran," Burns told a news briefing.
"He has also obstructed development of the Western-oriented defence structure in the Federation, and he's worked against a democratic Federation in general."

"While senior Bosnian officials have assured us that Mr Cengic will be replaced, the United States has decided that the $100 million worth of equipment ... will not be delivered to the Federation until Mr Cengic is relieved of his responsibilities formally and publicly," Burns said.

The bulk of the equipment, which includes tanks, artillery and helicopters, arrived last week by ship at the Croatian port of Ploce, but the vessel has since moved offshore pending resolution of the Cengic dispute.

The equipment is being supplied under a so-called "equip-and-train" programme whereby the United States hopes to bring the Federation up to the military level of the Bosnian Serbs, who heavily outgunned it during the Bosnian war.
The U.S. decision to go fully public with the demand for Cengic's head ratcheted up the pressure on Sarajevo following the failure so far of diplomatic efforts to oust him.

"I've been withholding his name for a week now because we have a commitment from the Bosnian government that he will be relieved of his duties, but we've not seen any action towards this," Burns said. Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic was told of U.S. concerns more than a week ago, he added.

Far from complying, Bosnia's Defence Ministry said Tuesday the U.S. demand had come "as a complete surprise" after U.S. President Bill Clinton certified in August that Bosnia had met all conditions for the equip-and-train programme to begin.
It said the new conditions "could give rise to suspicions developing between friendly nations which in the final analysis would not be beneficial for either of them".

U.S. officials have said they are also seeking the removal of another Bosnian Defence Ministry official who is a Croat, unlike the Moslem Cengic. They have not named the man or detailed their objections to him.

The officials have also spoken of outstanding problems in the Federation defence law, intended to unite Moslem and Croat forces, which was hammered together under U.S. pressure. But Burns said Cengic was the primary obstacle.
Burns gave no details of Cengic's alleged links with Iran, saying only that Tehran "to put it mildly, has no useful role to play in Bosnia" and that its involvement so far "has been quite negative."

Although supervised by a U.S. government official, James Pardew, equip-and-train is being carried out by a private U.S. firm. European countries have criticised the programme, saying it could increase the risk of renewed conflict in Bosnia.
